A Fatal Case of Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome
in a Patient with Stiff Leg Syndrome
Z. Nur Baykara*, Hiisnii Efendi**, Kamil Toker***
* Assoc. Prof. of Anaesthesiology, Faculty of Medicine, University of Kocaeli
** Prof. of Neurology, Faculty of Medicine, Univ of Kocaeli
‘ob Prof. of Anaesthesiology, Faculty of Medicine, University of Kocaeli
Summary
Stiff leg syndrome (SLS) is considered as a focal form of stiff
person syndrome (SPS) in which symptoms are confined to
a distal limb. A patient with stiff leg syndrome developed a
malignant neuroleptic syndrome (NMS) after having been
treated with a single dose of haloperidol. She developed
renal failure and disseminated intravascular coagulation,
and died despite extensive treatment. The potential vulner-
ability of patients with SPS/SLS to NMS is discussed.
Introduction
Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) is an autoimmune central ner-
vous system (CNS) disorder characterized by rigidity of trunk
and proximal limb muscles, episodic spasms and heightened
sensitivity to external stimuli [9, 26]. Continuous contrac-
tion of agonist and antagonist muscles caused by involun-
tary motor-unit firing at rest are the hallmark clinical and
electrophysiologic signs of the disease. SPS is thought to be
an autoimmune disorder because up to 60 % of patients have
antibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD 65),
the rate limiting enzyme for the synthesis of inhibitory neu-
rotransmitter y-aminobutyric acid (GABA), and association
with other autoimmune disorders. Stiff leg syndrome (SLS)
is considered as a focal form of SPS in which symptoms are
confined to a distal limb. In patients with SLS, abnormally

segmented electromyographic activity is recorded during
spasms in addition to the electrophysiologic findings of SPS
[12]. Even though the incidence of anti GAD 65 antibod-
ies and other pathological autoimmune findings is lower in
SLS, a significant overlap exist between SPS and SLS. The
clinical overlap is highlighted by the progression of some
patients with SLS into classic SPS [3, 12, 18].
About 0.7-1.4 % of patients receiving neuroleptic agents
tend to manifest the salient features of neuroleptic malignant
syndrome (NMS) including hyperpyrexia, severe rigidity,
altered mental status, elevated serum creatinine phospho-
kinase (CK), autonomic dysfunction, leukocytosis, and
extrapyramidal symptoms [29]. Despite its declining fre-
quency, NMS remains a significant source of morbidity and
mortality among patients receiving antipsychotics [24-25,
29}. Physicians should quickly diagnose this potentially
fatal and dose independent idiosyncratic reaction early and
manage it by aggressive supportive measures, by discon-
tinuation of offending drugs, and by the use of spesific drug
interventions.
The most common underlying conditions for which neu-
roleptics are used in NMS cases include affective disorders
and schizophrenia. However, NMS has also been observed
among patients who have organic brain disease, mental
retardation, delirium, acute catatonia, and extrapyramidal
disorders, and patients who have received neuroleptics or
dopamine depleting agents or have had dopamine agonists
abruptly withdrawn [24, 25].
We describe a case of the neuroleptic malignant syndrome

following a single injection of haloperidol in a patient who
has been diagnosed with SLS and reported 6 years ago [12].

According to our knowledge, there is no report on the com-
bination of both disorders.
Case Report
An 35-year-old woman presented to hospital due to pain-
ful spasms of her both legs, causing walking problems and
frequent falls. 6 years ago, due to progressive stiffness and
painful spasms of right leg elicited by leg movements and
emotional, auditory or tactile stimuli, presence of high titer
of anti-GAD 65 antibodies in her serum, and the typical
electrophysiological findings, she had been diagnosed as
SLS in another hospital. She had been prescribed clonaze-
pam 2 mg twice daily and her symptoms had been initially
improved substantially. About one year ago, her symptoms
came back and gradually evolved to both legs. During
the two months prior to her admission her symptoms had
become very severe. She was admitted to the hospital to
adjust the treatment.
On admission, she was well oriented and cooperative.
There were no signs of truncal rigidity or exaggerated
lumber lordosis. Both of the legs were rigid and painful.
Sudden tactile and auditory stimuli triggered spasms of the
legs. Motor examination of the legs could not be evaluated
because of the stiffness of the legs. Vibration sense was
reduced distally in the lower extremities. Motor and sensory
examinations were normal on the rest of the body. Patellar
jerk was hyperactive, but deep tendon reflexes on the upper
limbs were normal.
She have type | diabetes and her blood glucose was
poorly controlled despite insulin treatment. Her past medi-
cal history was remarkable for a diagnosis of hyperthyroi-
dism 15 years ago. She used propylthiouracil for 1 year
and remained euthyroid afterwards. She was diagnosed
with depression 6 months ago and started on venlafaxin.
Her daily medication on admission included clonazepam
(2 mg x 2), venlafaxin (75 mg x 1) and NPH insulin.
Blood chemistry examination revealed hyperglycemia
(203 mg.dL). Renal, hepatic function, electrolytes, chest-
X ray, electrocardiogram and urinalysis were normal. The
erythrocyte sedimentation rate was: 6 mm.h'!. Serum cerulo-
plasmin, copper, and B12 levels were within normal limits.
Insulin dosage was increased according to blood glucose
level. Magnetic resonance images (MRI) of the thoracic and
lumbar spine, and electroencephalogram were normal.
In the second day of hospital admission, she was given
5 mg of i.m. haloperidol for agitation. 5 mg of i.m. diazepam
was given due to painful spasms of her legs, 2 hours after
haloperidol administration. About 5 hours after haloperi-
dol administration, she had tremulousness and her speech
became dysarthric. Her temperature rose to 40.3 °C. She
was hypertensive (180/110 mmHg) and tachycardic (140/
min). Laboratory investigation revealed leukocytosis (leu-
kocyte count 21.1K.4~L"). Biochemical work-up showed:
glucose: 196 mg.dL"', K:6.5 mEg.L', SGOT: 30 U.L",
SGPT: 62 U.L', LDH:422 U.L', CK:1295 U.L'with nor-
mal CK MB fraction and cardiac troponin levels. Arterial
blood samples while breathing room air: pH:7.31, pO2:80.6
mmHg, pCO>:20.6 mmHg, standart HCO2:14.1 mmol.
L", base excess:-13.7 mmol.L. The levels of TSH, FT3
and FT4 were within normal limits. The insulin dose was
readjusted and the patient received vigorous hydration,
diuretic, and i.y. NaHCOs to alkalinize the urine and to
decrease potassium level. A lumbar puncture was per-

formed. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was clear and showed
no abnormalities. Blood, urine, CSF, and sputum samples
were collected for culture and she was started empirically
on ceftriaxone 2 g i.v. once daily. An electroencephalogram
showed diffuse slow waves consistent with encephalopathy.
MRI of the brain was normal. Cooling blankets and ice packs
were used to decrease temperature. Venlafaxin was stopped
and no further neuroleptic medication was used. The patient
was observed for the night. The next day, the patient had a
Glasgow coma score of 11, she developed lead pipe rigidity
and her elevated temperature persisted (38.5 °C), Her blood
pressure was labil. Her platelet count dropped down to 24K.
»L" (her initial platelet count was 271 K.wL"'). Prothrombin
time was borderline elevated, but the partial thromboplastin
time was normal as were levels of fibrinogen and D-dimer.
CK level climbed to 6845 U.L", SGOT level was 428 U.L",
SGPT level was 215 U.L"', and LDH level was: 422 U.L!
Urine myoglobin was positive. C-reactive protein value
(CRP) level was: 1.52 mg.L". Using serologic tests with the
following pathogens could be excluded: hepatitis A, B and C
virus, cytomegalovirus, Epstein Barr virus, human immune
deficiency virus, and herpes simplex virus 1. Antinuclear
antibody (ANA), anti-ds DNA, extractable nuclear antigen
(ENA) and RF were within normal limits. With the above
findings, the diagnosis of NMS was suggested and she was
transferred to the intensive care unit. Bromocriptin was ini
ated a dosage of 2.5 mg three times a day and was in ed
to 10 mg four times a day gradually. Because of abnormal
liver function test results, dantrolen sodium was not given.
Later that same week, the cultures came back negative.
A day later, she required intubation and ventilatory sup-
port for acute respiratory failure. A chest x-ray showed
marked fluid overload. Tracheal aspirate culture was nega-
tive. Continuous venovenous hemodiafiltration (CVVHDF)
was instituted due to oliguria, remarkable fluid accumula-
tion, exacerbated azotemia, and hyperpotasemia. Urine
myoglobin level was 1370 ng.mI' and the serum CK level
peaked at 104.136 U.L'. She developed complete anuria.
On the 3th day after the administration of haloperidol, the
antibiotic treatment was changed to piperacillin/tazobactam
2.25 g iv. every 8 hours, despite negative culture results.
Total parenteral nutrition was started. SGOT and SGPT lev-
els peaked at 3210 and 1892 U.L" respectively on the 5 th
day. Then, levels of CK, SGOT and SGPT started to decrease
and dropped down to 511, 54, and 69 U.L" respectively on
the 16 th day. Her trombosit level started to increase and
peaked at 231 K.wL’! on the 15 th day. However, her acute
renal failure did not improve and she remained anuric until
death. Coagulase-negative s. haemolyticus was isolated
from blood culture on the 11th day and it was considered
as indicative of contamination. Nevertheless, it was sensi-
tive to piperacillin/tazobactam which she used to take. She
developed overt disseminated intravascular coagulation on
the 19 th day after haloperidol administration, and despite
treatment, died four days later.
Discussion
This patient met the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of
Mental Disorders, Fourth Revision (DSM-IV) criteria for
NMS [2]. According to the DSM-IV criteria, the diagnosis
of NMS should be assigned only to patients who develop
severe muscle rigidity and elevated temperature while

receiving a neuroleptic drug and who display two or more of
the following signs and symptoms: diaphoresis, dysphagia,
tremor, incontinence, changes in level of consciousness,
mutism, tachycardia, elevated or labile blood pressure, leu-
kocytosis, and laboratory evidence of muscle injury.

Even though, pathophysiology of NMS is not fully under-
stood, neuroleptic induced dopamine blockade is considered
the chief mechanism mediating the symptoms of the syn-
drome. The blockade of central D2 receptors by neuroleptic
drugs in corpus striatum and hypothalamus is thought to
cause muscular rigidity and hyperthermia, which are main
signs of syndrome [24-25, 29]. Beyond these direct effects,
D2 receptor blockade might cause NMS by removing tonic
inhibition from the sympathetic nervous system [11]. The
resulting sympathoadrenal hyperactivity and dysregulation
leads to autonomic dysfunction. Other theories about its
pathophysiology have been proposed including imbalance
between dopaminergic activity and those of other transmit-
ters such as GABA and acetylcholine, central hyponatremia
and a kind of acute-phase reaction [27].
Many physiologic and environmental risk factors for the
development of NMS have been suggested: dehydration,
parenteral use of high potency antipsychotics (haloperidol,
fluphenazine), male gender. young age, uncontrolled diabe-
tes mellitus, exhaustion, excessive heat load, psychomotor
excitement, acute withdrawal of benzodiazepines and dopa-
mine agonists, sympathoadrenal hyperactivity and genetic
vulnerability, ie., -141 C Ins/Deél polymorphism [24-25,
29]. Our patient had some of the risk factors such as younger
age, poor controlled diabetes mellitus, and parenteral use of
high potency antipsychotic (haloperidol).
Successful treatment of this syndrome depends on
early recognition, and discontinuation of offending drugs.
Aggressive supportive measures including i.v, fluids,
antipyretic,and cooling blanket are required. Dopamine ago-
nists such as bromocriptin or amantadine appear to be effi-
cacious for NMS. Dantrolen sodium is administered to relax
peripheral muscles by inhibiting the release of calcium from
the sarcoplasmic reticulum of muscle. Hepatotoxic effects
may occur. Because of abnormal liver function test results,
dantrolen sodium was not given in this case. However,
according to a recent meta-analysis, no treatment regimen
including dantrolen could be considered as evidence based,
but dantrolen might be useful if premedication consisted
of a neuroleptic monotherapy and it is wise to discontinue
contributing medication even before the diagnosis of NMS
is definite [27].
The differential diagnosis of NMS should include in
particular serotonin syndrome in this Serotonin toxic-
ity results from an excess of serotonin in CNS, which can
be due to several different pharmacological mechanisms.
These include inhibition of the metabolism of serotonin
(monoamine oxidase inhibitors), prevention of the re-uptake
of serotonin in nerve terminals (selective serotonin reuptake
inhibitors {SSRIs}, tricyclics, tramadol, trazodone), and
increased serotonin precursors (triptans) or serotonin release
(serotonin releasing agents) [6]. Serotonin syndrome has
been increasingly recognized as a possible adverse event
in patients who receive SNRIs like venlafaxin [6, 8. 10,
17]. It is usually caused by the interaction of SNRIs and
another drug. NMS and serotonin syndrome are difficult to
differentiate because of their overlapping clinical features.
The diagnostic criteria for serotonin syndrome as proposed
by Sternbach are: recent change of a potent serotonin agent:

no history of substance abuse or infectious or metabolic
disease; absence of treatment with any antipsychotic drug;
and 23 of the following symptoms: change in the finding
of the mental status, agitation, myoclonus, hyperreflexia,
diaphoresis, shivering, tremor, diarrhea, uncoordination,
and fever [28]. Our patient has been using the same dose of
venlafaxine for six months and severe clinical manifesta-
tions developed following administration of haloperidol.
Based on these considerations and the presence of extrapy-
ramidal symptoms with lead pipe rigidity and severe clini-
cal manifestations favored a diagnosis of NMS rather than
serotonin syndrome. NMS has 10-20 % mortality rate. Even
though serotonin syndrome can be fatal, in most cases there
is a good prognosis when medication is discontinued. Only
23 deaths were reported until 1999 [22]. Serotonin syndrome
is associated with hyperkinesia, hyperreflexia and myoclo-
nus whereas akinesia, mutism, and extrapyramidal lead
pipe rigidity are seen in NMS. The are few cases of rhabdo-
myolysis associated with venlafaxin [13, 21]. Venlafaxin
also may cause NMS through SNRIs’s serotonergic inhibi-
tion of central dopaminergic activity, a mechanism similar
to extrapyramidal adverse drug reactions [17]. In this case,
this mechanism could have contributed to the catastrophic
progress of the NMS, rather than being responsible for the
syndrome, because of clinical manifestations disclosed fol-
lowing administration of the haloperidol. Haloperidol (a
classic neuroleptic drug), which is a strong blocker of D1,
D2 and @1 receptor and a weak blocker of 5 HT2A recep-
tors. Haloperidol (parenteral) was implicated as the most
common drug for NMS in 57 % of patients [14, 23].
One case report exists reporting a possible serotonin
syndrome following a single im. dose of haloperidol in
a patient who used to take venlafaxin [10]. Although the
hypothesis of NMS was first considered in that case, the
authors concluded that NMS was less probable due to the
poor response to spesific treatment(dantrolen) [10].
One could ask whether there is any interaction between
venlafaxin and haloperidol. Venlafaxin may increase halo-
peridol serum concentrations by decreasing its clearance. In
healthy subjects, venlafaxin reduced the clearance of single
oral 2 mg doses of haloperidol by 42 %, resulting in an 88 %
increased in Cmax and 70% increase in AUC; however,
the elimination half-life was unchanged [15]. The another
drug which the patient used to take was clonazepam. CNS
and/or respiratory depressant effects of clonazepam may be
additively or synergistically increased when used with ven-
lafaxin or haloperidol.
Further differential diagnoses of NMS include lethal
catatonia, anticholinergic delirium, malignant hyperthermia,
heat stroke, drug ingestions (e.g., sympathomimetics, anti-
cholinergics, lithium), seizures, sedative agent withdrawal,
central nervous system infections, sepsis, tetanus, and
midbrain structural lesions [24-25, 29]. Thorough physical
examination and laboratory tests including CK, electrolytes,
CBC count, blood culture, image studies of the head, and
lumbar puncture are recommended. However; no laboratory
abnormalities are specific or pathognomonic for the diagno-
sis; for this reason, it is hard to make an accurate diagnosis
until the syndrome is full blown.
Another issue one could consider is whether there is
a susceptibility to NMS in patients with SPS/SLS. Even

though this question can not be currently answered, some
comments still can be made. SLS may be regarded as
a focal variant of SPS or as a distinct entity [18]. Our
patient’s disease can be classified as a focal variant of SPS
due to presence of anti-GAD65 antibodies and associated
comorbidities including insulin dependent diabetes mel-
litus and thyroid disease [18]. The level of GABA appears
reduced in CSF and certain brain regions of patients with
SPS [16]. It was also claimed that in addition to dopamine
hypoactivity, there is a GABAergic deficiency in the patho-

106 Baykara, Efendi, Toker: A Fatal Case of Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome in a Patient with Stiff Leg Syndrome
physiology of NMS [7, 20]. In a previous study, various
cerebrospinal fluid parameters were measured in 11 patients
with NMS and compared them with 8 age matched controls
[20]. Concentrations of homovanillic acid and GABA were
significantly lower in cerebrospinal fluid of patients with
NMS than in the controls [20]. GABAA agonists have also
been shown to alleviate NMS [7]. Even though, the level of
GABA in CSF was not measured in our patient, since she
had high titer of anti-GAD 65 antibodies in her serum, it
might be low. GABAergic deficiency might have made the
patient more vulnerable to neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
As mentioned above, dysregulated sympathetic nervous sys-
tem overactivity is a core component of neuroleptic malig-
nant syndrome and peripheral catecholamines are typically
elevated [11]. The tonic inhibitory inputs are translated to
preganglionic sympathetic neurons by way of dopaminergic
hypothalamospinal tracts. Interruption of these inhibitory
inputs by neuroleptic: ses dysregulated sympathetic ner-
vous system hyperactivity. A liability to sympathetic ner-
vous system hyperactivation and/ or dysfunction in response
to emotional or physiological stress may constitute a vulner-
ability for NMS, which, when coupled with state variables
such as dopamin receptor antagoniSm or acute psychic dis-
tress cause the clinical syndrome of NMS [11]. Autonomic
hyperactivity including hypertension, tachycardia and agita-
tion during muscle spasm has been described in SPS [19].
The periventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus, which pro-
ject to the structures of the autonomic core including inter-
mediolateral cell column of the spinal cord and ventrolateral
medulla, are intensely innervated by GABA-ergic axons
arising from the limbic system. It has been claimed that
autonomic hyperactivity in SPS might have been secondary
to an impairment of GABA-ergic pathways [19]. Autonomic
hyperactivity in patients with SLS has not been described
previously, but it might be expected in the focal variant type
SLS. No signs of autonomic hyperactivity were observed in
our patient before the cerastropiie process, but they might
have been overlooked. Altogether, disturbance of inhibitory
GABA-ergic pathways in SLS may have made the patient
more vulnerable to neuroleptic malignant syndrome. It
remains to be investigated. The present rigidity, spasms and
agitation might also have contributed to the development of
clinical picture of severe NMS in our patient.
Complication of NMS are renal failure, aspiration pneu-
monia, arrhythmias, respiratory failure, thrombocytopenia,
hypovolemic shock, deep venous thrombosis, pulmonary
embolism, myocardial infarction, seizures, severe liver
failure, sepsisemia and DIC [1, 4, 24, 25]. Even though,
death usually results from respiratory failure, cardiovascu-
lar collapse, myoglobinuric renal failure, arrhythmias, or
diffuse intravascular coagulation (DIC), renal failure is the
most common cause of death in NMS. Renal failure is a
strong predictor of mortality, representing a mortality risk
of approximately 50 % [1, 4].

and died despite extensive treatment. The potential vulner-

was hypertensive (180/110 mmHg) and tachycardic (140/
min). Laboratory investigation revealed leukocytosis (leu-
kocyte count 21.1K.4~L"). Biochemical work-up showed:
glucose: 196 mg.dL"', K:6.5 mEg.L', SGOT: 30 U.L",
SGPT: 62 U.L', LDH:422 U.L', CK:1295 U.L'with nor-
mal CK MB fraction and cardiac troponin levels. Arterial
blood samples while breathing room air: pH:7.31, pO2:80.6
mmHg, pCO>:20.6 mmHg, standart HCO2:14.1 mmol.
L", base excess:-13.7 mmol.L. The levels of TSH, FT3
and FT4 were within normal limits. The insulin dose was
readjusted and the patient received vigorous hydration,
diuretic, and i.y. NaHCOs to alkalinize the urine and to
decrease potassium level. A lumbar puncture was per-

segments.text:
formed. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was clear and showed
no abnormalities. Blood, urine, CSF, and sputum samples
were collected for culture and she was started empirically
on ceftriaxone 2 g i.v. once daily. An electroencephalogram
showed diffuse slow waves consistent with encephalopathy.
MRI of the brain was normal. Cooling blankets and ice packs
were used to decrease temperature. Venlafaxin was stopped
and no further neuroleptic medication was used. The patient
was observed for the night. The next day, the patient had a
Glasgow coma score of 11, she developed lead pipe rigidity
and her elevated temperature persisted (38.5 °C), Her blood
pressure was labil. Her platelet count dropped down to 24K.
»L" (her initial platelet count was 271 K.wL"'). Prothrombin
time was borderline elevated, but the partial thromboplastin
time was normal as were levels of fibrinogen and D-dimer.
CK level climbed to 6845 U.L", SGOT level was 428 U.L",
SGPT level was 215 U.L"', and LDH level was: 422 U.L!
Urine myoglobin was positive. C-reactive protein value
(CRP) level was: 1.52 mg.L". Using serologic tests with the
following pathogens could be excluded: hepatitis A, B and C
virus, cytomegalovirus, Epstein Barr virus, human immune
deficiency virus, and herpes simplex virus 1. Antinuclear
antibody (ANA), anti-ds DNA, extractable nuclear antigen
(ENA) and RF were within normal limits. With the above
findings, the diagnosis of NMS was suggested and she was
transferred to the intensive care unit. Bromocriptin was ini
ated a dosage of 2.5 mg three times a day and was in ed
to 10 mg four times a day gradually. Because of abnormal
liver function test results, dantrolen sodium was not given.
Later that same week, the cultures came back negative.
A day later, she required intubation and ventilatory sup-
port for acute respiratory failure. A chest x-ray showed
marked fluid overload. Tracheal aspirate culture was nega-
tive. Continuous venovenous hemodiafiltration (CVVHDF)
was instituted due to oliguria, remarkable fluid accumula-
tion, exacerbated azotemia, and hyperpotasemia. Urine
myoglobin level was 1370 ng.mI' and the serum CK level
peaked at 104.136 U.L'. She developed complete anuria.
On the 3th day after the administration of haloperidol, the
antibiotic treatment was changed to piperacillin/tazobactam
2.25 g iv. every 8 hours, despite negative culture results.
Total parenteral nutrition was started. SGOT and SGPT lev-
els peaked at 3210 and 1892 U.L" respectively on the 5 th
day. Then, levels of CK, SGOT and SGPT started to decrease
and dropped down to 511, 54, and 69 U.L" respectively on
the 16 th day. Her trombosit level started to increase and
peaked at 231 K.wL’! on the 15 th day. However, her acute
renal failure did not improve and she remained anuric until
death. Coagulase-negative s. haemolyticus was isolated
from blood culture on the 11th day and it was considered
as indicative of contamination. Nevertheless, it was sensi-
tive to piperacillin/tazobactam which she used to take. She
developed overt disseminated intravascular coagulation on
the 19 th day after haloperidol administration, and despite
treatment, died four days later.

This patient met the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of
Mental Disorders, Fourth Revision (DSM-IV) criteria for
NMS [2].

segments.text:
Our patient had some of the risk factors such as younger
age, poor controlled diabetes mellitus, and parenteral use of
high potency antipsychotic (haloperidol).
segments.evidence: Deterministic clinical-window selection for Stage 07 single-case v1.

segments.text:
No signs of autonomic hyperactivity were observed in
our patient before the cerastropiie process, but they might
have been overlooked. Altogether, disturbance of inhibitory
GABA-ergic pathways in SLS may have made the patient
more vulnerable to neuroleptic malignant syndrome. It
remains to be investigated. The present rigidity, spasms and
agitation might also have contributed to the development of
clinical picture of severe NMS in our patient.
